blogs.title: Only the Commissioner Can Seek MPWA ‘Average Daily Wage’ Penalties
blogs.description: The Eighth Circuit held that Minn. Stat. § 181.101 authorizes only the Commissioner—not private plaintiffs—to seek average daily wage penalties, even though employees may sue for unpaid wages under § 181.171. The panel’s textualist reading leaned on statutory structure, the Commissioner’s demand-and-collect mechanism in § 181.101(a), and the Legislature’s choice to expressly grant private penalty rights in other sections (e.g., §§ 181.13, 181.14). The post will unpack the opinion’s reliance on Minnesota interpretive canons and decisions like Allan and Milner, reconcile Hull v. ConvergeOne, and explore practical consequences for wage litigation strategy in Minnesota.

blogs.title: Laidlaw, Voluntary Cessation, and MFLSA Civil Penalties: A Standing and Mootness Rubicon
blogs.description: After Consilio paid wages and liquidated damages, Cohen pressed for MFLSA statutory penalties—payable to the Commissioner—raising Article III questions the Eighth Circuit flagged sua sponte. Citing Laidlaw, the court recognized civil penalties can redress injury through deterrence, but vacated and remanded for a threshold determination whether the claim is moot depending on whether the challenged overtime policy persists. This post analyzes the Laidlaw deterrence rationale, Town of Chester’s requirement of standing for each form of relief, the heavy burden on defendants under voluntary cessation, and Judge Kobes’s concurrence questioning whether Laidlaw extends to MFLSA penalties. It also maps the factual showings each side should build on remand to win the jurisdictional fight.

blogs.title: Pleading Precision Matters: MWTA Penalties and Late-Shifted Injunctive Relief
blogs.description: Cohen’s MWTA notice-change claim failed because he stipulated he’d been fully paid and offered no statutory authority for civil penalties—an underdeveloped argument the Eighth Circuit treated as waived. Separately, the court refused to consider a new request for an affirmative injunction (rescinding the 2019 policy) raised for the first time at summary judgment, citing the rule that new claims belong in amended complaints. This post distills procedural lessons: preserve injunctive theories early, anchor MWTA claims in concrete remedial provisions, and avoid swapping remedies midstream if you want to keep jurisdictional hooks and settlement leverage intact.

blogs.title: Minnesota’s Wage Enforcement Architecture After Cohen: Private Suits, Public Penalties, and Litigation Strategy
blogs.description: Cohen spotlights Minnesota’s hybrid enforcement design: employees can privately recover wages and MFLSA liquidated damages, but penalties under key provisions flow through the Commissioner. The court’s MPWA holding curtails private leverage rooted in § 181.101 penalties, while the MFLSA remand leaves open whether deterrence-based standing can sustain claims for penalties payable to the state. This post surveys how that architecture shapes class and individual case strategy, employer efforts to moot claims by paying back wages, and the importance of parallel agency engagement and properly pleaded injunctive relief to keep live controversies when policies remain in force.
